title: Frontier LLM Tier List
subtitle: A personal, time-indexed ranking of frontier models.

changes.label: Initial placements
changes.note: My initial tier list based on countless hours of usage

model.name: GPT-5.2
model.summary: Exceptional instruction following and long-term agentic capabilities
model.reasoning: This is the smartest model at the moment, in terms of raw intelligence and reasoning capabilities. Others don't even come close in programming and math. It is so obvious once you actually use it for anything complex enough that it was really weird for me to see most people prefer Opus 4.5 instead.

model.name: GPT-5.2-Codex
model.summary: Worse than GPT-5.2 in general, but more efficient when working with code
model.reasoning: This is a good model, but it feels overtuned in a way that actually makes it worse than GPT-5.2 in instruction following. I saw some people having a similar experience with it. I personally don't really use it, and always prefer GPT-5.2.

model.name: Opus 4.5
model.summary: Good and fast chat model that also has some taste
model.reasoning: I don't use it for code as GPT-5.2 is far superior, but it's a nice chat model that reminds me of GPT-4o in a good way and it's smart enough for daily usage in random questions. It also works well with text and with design if you explain to it the vibe you want.

model.name: Gemini 3 Pro
model.summary: Has some raw intelligence but is unusable in practice
model.reasoning: I really tried to believe that it is a good model. But I just can't get anything useful out of it really. I still believe that it has raw intelligence in it, but Google just can't do proper post-train yet and this model is just really unusable. It doesn't follow instructions in the same way Gemini 2.5 didn't, and it is very lazy and doesn't want to think at all, even for the hardest questions. It doesn't think deeply about things unless you start handholding it. I don't recommend it for anything.

model.name: Sonnet 4.5
model.reasoning: Opus 4.5 is not much more expensive and delivers far better results, so I don't see any point in using Sonnet 4.5 unless you're seeking some cost efficiency, but in that case there are better options than Anthropic.

changes.label: New Codex and Opus
changes.note: Anthropic released Claude Opus 4.6, and OpenAI almost immediately responded with GPT-5.3-Codex

model.name: GPT-5.3-Codex
model.summary: Very fast and efficient coding model with quality close to the best
model.reasoning: I didn't really like GPT-5.2-Codex, but this new version is actually noticeably better. It still lacks the extreme instruction following and long-term coherence that GPT-5.2 has, but it's better than GPT-5.2-Codex in this regard, while also being much faster and more efficient. I'm now using it alongside GPT-5.2 in Codex, depending on the task.

model.name: Opus 4.6
model.summary: Nice and fast chat model with some taste
model.reasoning: I still don't use it for code, as GPT-5.2 and GPT-5.3-Codex are far superior. But I'm still using Opus for daily chatting, prompt writing and design discussions. It doesn't *feel* much different from the previous version, but the quality seems to be noticeably better.

Opus 4.6 is not much more expensive and delivers far better results. Waiting for Sonnet 5, but even then I don't think I'll be using it instead of Opus, as I value the size of the model for this case.

changes.label: Sparks of joy
changes.note: OpenAI released their first Cerebras-served model: GPT-5.3-Codex-Spark

model.name: GPT-5.3-Codex-Spark
model.reasoning: This model is just pure speed. And after seeing it, I thought that it would work great for very long iterative plans. But this model is just too lazy and always tries to cut corners, simply like other Codex models, but even worse. However, I found it very cool for highly parallelizable narrow tasks with well-defined instructions. Some things that would take a few hours now can be done in 15 minutes.

model.name: Sonnet 4.6
model.summary: Cheaper alternative with quality similar to Opus
model.reasoning: I still don't see much sense in using Sonnet over Opus apart from cost optimization. But this one turned out to be slightly better. For front-end and design it gave me results on par with Opus 4.6. Might be worth it sometimes.

changes.label: .1 updates
changes.note: OpenAI released GPT-5.4, Google released Gemini 3.1 Pro

model.name: Gemini 3.1 Pro
model.reasoning: To be honest, I didn't play around with this model as much as I did with others in this list, but I tried it for some front-end design, and some bug hunting as well. I noticed that it thinks more than 3.0 and its design skills definitely improved. But I still don't see how this model can be used for real work. In my attempts it started going in loops and not finishing, eventually eating all my OpenRouter credits while trying to complete a given task. It still loses to GPT and Claude models in most things, and probably one of the few things that it is actually good at is world knowledge and humor. But these aren't that useful in things I'm doing for work.

model.name: GPT-5.4
model.summary: Most intelligent and useful model overall
model.reasoning: Deep in my soul I hoped for GPT-5.3 or GPT-5.4 to be an even more thorough version of GPT-5.2 that already had some extreme level of instruction following and long-term coherence. Then with GPT-5.3-Codex I felt like a good efficient model is often nicer to work with compared to a more flawless but much slower and much weirder one like GPT-5.2. Plus it felt more creative compared to robotic GPT-5.2. GPT-5.4 took that path too. In general, it is closer to GPT-5.3-Codex than to GPT-5.2 in many ways. It's efficient, it's more creative, it's less robotic. It still feels less thorough than GPT-5.2, but all the creativeness and efficiency pros outweigh this, so this is now my go-to model for code and any reasoning tasks.

model.name: Opus 4.7
model.reasoning:
This feels like a minor incremental release with no major changes in behavior or usefulness. It is still a nice, fast chat model with some taste. I don't see a meaningful change in what I would use it for compared to Opus 4.6.

It is still more tasteful than other models in most cases. At the same time, it is very hard to work with in complex scenarios with lots of context and instructions. It loses track, doesn't follow what you ask, and generally produces bad results.

The thing I liked most was Claude Design. Its rate limits are extremely tight even on the $200 subscription, and it still has the same behavior issues that make larger design projects hard to finish.

model.name: GPT-5.5
model.reasoning:
This is a significant release. The model became more expensive, though the higher price is mostly offset by better token efficiency and stronger results. The Pro version can often finish a task in 5 minutes instead of 20 minutes. Its Codex variant, even on High reasoning effort, is very dynamic and nice to use in real time when developing something.

I don't notice any major new abilities, so it does not feel dramatically smarter in that sense. The model is *bigger* and feels *bigger*, even if the jump is smaller than GPT-4.5 felt in its era. I'm now using it on High or Medium in most of my personal use cases, while leaving XHigh for massive parallel workflows that don't suffer from being slow.

It still has very bad design taste and all the rigid GPT-5.x traits.

model.name: GPT-5.6 Sol
model.summary: Faster, smarter, and better in general
model.reasoning:
An incredible model. It is faster and smarter than previous GPTs were, and even less autistic. That model and Codex are so good that you can just throw anything at it. Overall I've noticed a clear progression from 5.2 -> 5.3/5.4 -> 5.5 -> 5.6. With every iteration, the models became more capable in most cases, more token efficient, less autistic, and nicer to use. These updates also didn't really hurt performance in other areas, except for some specific case degradations in the 5.2 -> 5.3 update. Max reasoning effort in 5.6 still allows it to think for a lot of time on hard problems.

What I'm feeling with 5.6 Sol in Codex right now is that it's basically almost an ASI-level slave robot that can do anything. I'm delegating more and more things to it. Codex planned the entire Europe trip for me, it booked things for me, and was very helpful during the trip in everyday questions, timing and plan changes.

The single most noticeable pain point is now the speed when it works as an agent and needs to perform a lot of actions. Model intelligence crossed the general usefulness threshold for me, and with the upcoming Cerebras fast mode I expect the user experience to cross it too. The only thing preventing the near-flawless usage of Codex was that I had to wait sometimes a few minutes while it was searching the web, reading our files, and thinking. If that work is done in a few seconds rather than minutes, it becomes a pretty universal system that I'll use even more for a lot of things.

model.name: Fable 5
model.summary: Bigger than ever, but still Claude
model.reasoning:
This model is great. It's mostly what I expected from the release: a bigger Claude. It still has mostly the same personality, same taste and traits. It's annoying in the same way Sonnet and Opus are, but it's just smarter, which makes it noticeably nicer to use. It writes good code, and is capable of doing things GPT is also capable of in terms of intelligence.

But it's not perfect. It's slow, it's expensive, and it's Claude. The UI/UX design capabilities are better than ever. On my small tests it produced the best results so far, with near-perfect execution of what I've asked for and a good understanding of the intent and vibe. I couldn't use it much for security work because of safety refusals.

I'm still using it often as a chat-only model, the same way I used previous Claude models. It just doesn't click for me for anything else. It's too annoying and tries too much to be "your friend Claude".
